A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the excess lung cancer among the nickel workers was likely due to the presence of PAHs, and possibly other gaseous and particulate contaminants, which were associated with the smelting and refining of nickel/copper.
the epidemiologic findings and the industrial hygiene follow-up investigation were mutually supportive.
PAHs are the probable cause of the excess lung cancers observed in the nickel/copper smelting and refining workers in Ontario.
The main takeaway from our work is that

an industrial hygiene follow-back study can help explain the cause of an excess disease finding in an epidemiologic study and that such a study can be used to identify potential exposures to carcinogens.
industrial hygiene investigations can be useful in helping to explain epidemiologic findings, and in identifying potential causes of disease.

an occupational health and safety follow-up assessment of a statistically significant finding in a cohort study can be an effective tool for identifying a possible cause of disease and for developing appropriate prevention and intervention strategies.
